definition: Dissuade means to persuade someone not to do something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word dissuade. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know dissuade should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her counselor tried to dissuade her from dropping the chemistry course just one week before the final.
Discourage is milder than dissuade; you can discourage someone with a frown, but dissuading them means actually convincing them not to act.
Prevent is stronger than dissuade because it stops the action entirely, while a dissuaded person still freely chooses not to act.

To deter is to discourage action through obstacles or the fear of consequences - alarms, penalties, and guard dogs deter, and they work on anything that can hesitate, even animals. To dissuade works only through persuasion: reasons and argument that change a person's mind. A guard dog deters; a worried friend dissuades.

To talk someone out of something is the casual, conversational way to say you convinced them not to do it. Dissuade is its formal register: the word a report or a news story would use for the same feat. A friend talks you out of a bad haircut; a counselor dissuades a student from quitting.

To counsel against something is to formally advise that it not be done - the act is the advice itself, which may well be ignored. To dissuade is to succeed: the person actually changes their mind and holds back. A lawyer can counsel against the deal all week; she has dissuaded her client only when he walks away.

Dissuade means to persuade someone not to do something.
A storm warning flashed across the news just as Lena grabbed her keys for a midnight drive up the mountain.
Her parents laid out the forecast, the icy switchbacks, and the closed ranger stations one by one.
In the end they dissuaded her from going, and she left safely at dawn instead.
The parents did not forbid the trip or take the keys; they used reasons and evidence to convince Lena not to go, which is exactly what dissuade means.
Dissuade almost always takes 'from': you dissuade someone from doing something, usually through reasons and argument rather than force.
It is the direct opposite of persuade, which shares the same Latin root; persuade urges someone toward an action, while dissuade urges them away from it.

When the board of the Harwick Museum met in March, one agenda line overshadowed all the rest: sell the collection's only Turner seascape to pay for urgent roof repairs.
Elena Voss, the curator, did not shout, plead, or threaten to resign.
She arrived with a folder of figures instead.
Admission revenue, she showed the trustees, rose eleven percent whenever the Turner was on display, and three regional schools had built their spring art programs around visits to it.
Selling the painting, she argued, would patch one roof and then quietly drain the museum's income for a decade to come.
By the final vote her case had done its work: Voss had dissuaded the board, and the trustees rejected the sale nine to one, approving a modest loan for the repairs instead.
